summary: Describes a way to mix a preshared key into the IKEv2 key exchange so VPN traffic stays protected even if quantum computers later break today's key exchange. It addresses the risk of someone recording VPN traffic now and decrypting it later.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8784 gives IKEv2 a way to survive the arrival of a quantum computer. Two peers that already share a long secret mix that secret into the keys they derive, so an attacker who records the traffic and later breaks the Diffie-Hellman part still cannot read the recorded session. The existing authentication stays in place; the shared secret only strengthens it.

questions: how to make ikev2 post-quantum secure
what is ikev2 preshared key mixing
what is a ppk in ikev2
should i use a group ppk
subtitle: Mixing an extra preshared key into IKEv2 so that VPN traffic stays protected even if quantum computers break today's key exchange.

tldr.problem: A quantum computer large enough to matter would break the Diffie-Hellman exchange inside IKEv2, which would expose recorded VPN traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a second shared secret, a post-quantum preshared key, and runs three of the IKEv2 subkeys through the pseudorandom function a second time with that secret as the key. New notifications tell both sides which secret is in use.
tldr.outcome: If the shared secret is strong enough, the keys that protect the tunnel are safe from a quantum attack even after the traffic has been recorded, without changing how IKEv2 authenticates the peers.

today: RFC 8784 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It registers the USE_PPK, PPK_IDENTITY and NO_PPK_AUTH status notifications for IKEv2, along with the IKEv2 Post-quantum Preshared Key ID Types registry.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Recent achievements in developing quantum computers show that it is probably feasible to build one that is cryptographically significant. If such a computer were implemented, many of the cryptographic algorithms and protocols in use today would be insecure. A quantum computer would be able to solve Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman problems in polynomial time, which would mean the security of existing IKEv2 systems would be compromised.

IKEv1, when used with strong preshared keys, is not vulnerable to quantum attacks, because those keys are one of the inputs to the key derivation function. If the preshared key has sufficient entropy and the pseudorandom function, encryption and authentication transforms are quantum secure, the resulting system is believed to be quantum secure, meaning secure against classical attackers of today and against future attackers with a quantum computer.

This document describes a way to give IKEv2 a similar property: assuming that the two end systems share a long secret key, the resulting exchange is quantum secure. Bringing post-quantum security to IKEv2 removes the need to use an obsolete version of IKE to reach that goal.

The general idea is to add a secret shared between the initiator and the responder, in addition to the authentication method already provided within IKEv2. This secret is stirred into the SK_d value, which is used to generate the key material for the child security associations and the SKEYSEED for the IKE security associations created when the initial IKE security association is rekeyed. The secret provides quantum resistance to the IPsec security associations and to any subsequent IKE security associations. It is also stirred into the SK_pi and SK_pr values, which allows both sides to detect a secret mismatch cleanly.

It was considered important to minimize the changes to IKEv2. The existing mechanisms for authentication and key exchange remain in place, so the protocol continues to perform the Diffie-Hellman exchange and, if configured, public key authentication. The document does not replace the authentication checks the protocol does; it strengthens them by using an additional secret key.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, two VPN endpoints agree on a key by exchanging numbers over the network and doing arithmetic on them. A powerful quantum computer could undo that arithmetic later, from a recording. The fix in this RFC is that the endpoints already share a secret that never crosses the network, and that secret is folded into the keys they derive. Recording the traffic is no longer enough.

sections.title: What Each Peer Needs
sections.content:
Each IKE peer is assumed to have a list of post-quantum preshared keys, along with their identifiers, and any potential initiator selects which one to use with a specific responder. Implementations also have a configurable flag that determines whether this key is mandatory for the peer in question.

The key is independent of the preshared key, if any, that the IKEv2 protocol uses for authentication, because the preshared key in IKEv2 is not used for any key derivation and therefore does not protect against quantum computers.

The configuration assumed to be on each node consists of the tuple: peer, key, key identifier, and whether it is mandatory. The document assumes the reader is familiar with the payload notation defined in Section 1.2 of RFC 7296.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router needs a table: which peer it talks to, which secret it shares with that peer, the name of that secret, and whether the secret has to be used. The flag is what makes the deployment safe to roll out in stages.

sections.title: The Exchange
sections.content:
If the initiator is configured to use a post-quantum preshared key with the responder, whether or not its use is mandatory, it must include a USE_PPK notification in the IKE_SA_INIT request. USE_PPK is a status notification with the type 16435, a protocol ID of 0, no Security Parameter Index and no notification data. If the initiator has to resend that message with a COOKIE notification, the resend includes USE_PPK if the original did.

If the responder does not support the specification or has no such key configured, it ignores the notification, as it would any unknown status notification, and continues with IKEv2 as normal. Otherwise it replies with its IKE_SA_INIT message including a USE_PPK notification.

When the initiator receives the reply it checks whether the responder included USE_PPK. If it did not and the mandatory flag says that using these keys is mandatory for this responder, the initiator must abort the exchange, which happens when the initiator believes it has a mandatory key and the responder either does not support them or has none configured for the initiator. If using a key for this responder is optional, the initiator continues with IKEv2 as normal, without the keys.

If the responder did include USE_PPK, the initiator selects a key and its identifier, and computes a modification of the standard IKEv2 key derivation from Section 2.14 of RFC 7296:

SKEYSEED = prf(Ni | Nr, g^ir)
{SK_d' | SK_ai | SK_ar | SK_ei | SK_er | SK_pi' | SK_pr'}
                = prf+ (SKEYSEED, Ni | Nr | SPIi | SPIr)

SK_d  = prf+ (PPK, SK_d')
SK_pi = prf+ (PPK, SK_pi')
SK_pr = prf+ (PPK, SK_pr')

The standard derivation is used unchanged, except that the three resulting subkeys SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr, shown with primes in the formula, are then run through the pseudorandom function again, this time using the shared secret as the key. The unprimed versions of these keys are used as inputs to the subsequent steps of the exchange.

Using the prf+ construction ensures that it is always possible to get resulting keys of the same size as the initial ones, even if the underlying pseudorandom function has an output size different from its key size. All the pseudorandom functions currently defined for IKEv2 have an output size equal to their preferred key size, so for those only the first iteration of prf+ is needed: SK_d = prf(PPK, SK_d' | 0x01), and likewise for SK_pi and SK_pr.

The shared secret is used in the SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr calculations only during the initial IKE security association setup. It must not be used when these subkeys are calculated as the result of a rekey, resumption or similar operations.

The initiator then sends the IKE_AUTH request, including the key identifier in a PPK_IDENTITY notification, which is a status notification with the type 16436, a protocol ID of 0, no SPI and notification data consisting of the identifier PPK_ID. A responder may have some keys but not the one the initiator named. In that case it cannot continue with the key, and in particular cannot authenticate the initiator, but it could continue with ordinary IKEv2 if the initiator supplied authentication data computed the ordinary way. For that purpose, if using the keys is optional for the initiator, the initiator must include a NO_PPK_AUTH notification in the same message. NO_PPK_AUTH is a status notification with the type 16437, a protocol ID of 0 and no SPI, and its data holds the initiator's authentication data computed using SK_pi', which was computed without the shared secret. Because the notification carries no authentication method field, the method used must be the one indicated in the AUTH payload. Including this notification means the initiator computes its authentication data twice, which may cost power when digital signatures are involved.

The responder decrypts and checks the message with SK_ei and SK_ai, then looks for the key identifier in the PPK_IDENTITY notification. If there is no PPK_IDENTITY notification and the peers did exchange USE_PPK notifications, the responder must return an AUTHENTICATION_FAILED notification and fail the negotiation. If the notification carries a key identifier the responder does not know, or one not configured for the identity in the IDi payload, the responder checks whether the keys are mandatory and whether the initiator sent NO_PPK_AUTH. If the keys are mandatory or no NO_PPK_AUTH was sent, the responder must return AUTHENTICATION_FAILED and fail the negotiation. Otherwise it may continue with ordinary IKEv2, using the data from the NO_PPK_AUTH notification as the initiator's authentication data.

When a key is in use, the responder extracts it and computes SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr with the same formulas, continues with the IKE_AUTH exchange validating the AUTH payload as usual, and sends a reply that includes a PPK_IDENTITY notification with no data to indicate that the key is in use. When the initiator receives the reply it checks for that notification. If it receives one, it marks the security association as using the configured key to generate the three subkeys, and the content of the received notification must be ignored. If it does not receive one, it must either fail the negotiation with an AUTHENTICATION_FAILED notification in an INFORMATIONAL exchange, if the key was configured as mandatory, or continue without the key, if the key was optional and the initiator sent NO_PPK_AUTH in the request.

With EAP the initiator does not include the AUTH payload in the first request, and the responder sends its AUTH payload back in the first reply; the peers exchange AUTH payloads once EAP succeeds, so the responder sends the AUTH payload twice while the initiator sends it once. The general rule, which covers EAP, is that the initiator includes a PPK_IDENTITY notification, and optionally a NO_PPK_AUTH, in the request message that contains the AUTH payload. In the EAP case the responder always computes the AUTH payload in the first IKE_AUTH reply without the shared secret, because PPK_ID is not yet known to it, and once the request carrying PPK_IDENTITY arrives it follows the rules above.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange has three notifications. The initiator says it wants to use a shared secret, the responder says whether it has one, and then the initiator names which one it is using. Three of the derived keys are then run through the pseudorandom function a second time with the shared secret, so an attacker who learns the Diffie-Hellman value still cannot compute them. The initiator can also offer a fallback authentication, in case the responder turns out not to have the named secret.

sections.title: Rolling the Change Out
sections.content:
The algorithm was designed so that someone can introduce these keys into an existing IKE network without causing disruption. In the initial phase, the administrator visits each node and configures the set of keys and identifiers it needs to know, the key that will be used for each peer it will initiate to, and the value false for the mandatory flag for each peer it initiates to, so that using the keys is not yet mandatory.

With that configuration a node keeps working with nodes that have not been upgraded. The USE_PPK and NO_PPK_AUTH notifications make this work: an initiator that has not been upgraded sends no USE_PPK, so the responder knows the peers will not use a key; a responder that has not been upgraded sends no USE_PPK, so the initiator knows not to use one. If both peers have been upgraded but the responder has no key configured for the initiator, the responder can still continue with ordinary IKEv2 if the initiator sent a NO_PPK_AUTH notification. If both are upgraded and configured, they both realise it, and the child security associations become quantum secure.

As an optional second step, once all nodes have been upgraded, the administrator goes back through the nodes and marks the use of a key as mandatory. This does not change the strength against a passive attacker, but it does mean that an active attacker with a quantum computer fast enough to break the Diffie-Hellman exchange in real time cannot perform a downgrade attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The design lets you add these keys one router at a time. Each router learns whether the other side supports them by the notification in the reply, and falls back to the ordinary exchange when it does not. Only after every router has been converted is it worth making the key mandatory, which closes a downgrade attack.

sections.title: The Key and Its Identifier
sections.content:
Both the initiator and the responder must have the secret value, with the responder selecting the key based on the identifier the initiator sends. Both are configured with fixed key and identifier values and perform the lookup on the identifier. Later specifications are expected to extend this to allow dynamically changing key values, so the identifier the initiator sends has its first octet set to a type value.

Two types are defined. PPK_ID_OPAQUE (1) means that the format of the identifier, and of the key itself, is not specified by this document; it is assumed to be mutually intelligible by both sides. This type is intended for implementations that choose not to disclose the type of key to active attackers. PPK_ID_FIXED (2) means that the identifier and the key are fixed octet strings, with the remaining bytes of the identifier being a configured value, and a fixed mapping between identifier and key configured locally on both sides. Not all implementations can configure arbitrary octet strings, so to improve interoperability it is recommended that in the PPK_ID_FIXED case both the key and the identifier be limited to the base64 character set.

Identifiers of the type PPK_ID_FIXED, and the corresponding keys, are assumed to be configured within the device out of band. RFC 6030 describes a format for the transport and provisioning of symmetric keys, which could be reused with its PIN profile, using the identifier as the Id attribute and the key as the Secret element.

The document does not require the key to be unique for each pair of peers. If it is, the solution provides full peer authentication, but each host then needs as many independent keys as peers it talks to, and that does not scale. It is possible to use a single key for a group of users. Since each peer also uses classical public key cryptography, group members can neither impersonate each other nor read each other's traffic unless they use quantum computers to break public key operations. However, group members can record traffic they have access to and decrypt it later, and a key known to a large group is more susceptible to theft, since an attacker with a quantum computer who gets the group key reveals all the communications inside the group. For these reasons, using a group key is not recommended.

Combining a group key with PPK-only authentication is also not recommended, because in that case any member of the group can impersonate any other member without the help of quantum computers. PPK-only authentication can be achieved in IKEv2 by using the NULL Authentication method of RFC 7619. Without a shared key the NULL method gives no authentication of the peers, but since the key is stirred into SK_pi and SK_pr, the peers become authenticated when a key is in use. Using these keys must be mandatory for peers that advertise support for them in IKE_SA_INIT and use NULL authentication. And since the peers are authenticated through the key, the ID Type in the IDi and IDr payloads should not be ID_NULL, even though the NULL authentication method is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier names which secret to use, and its first octet says how it is formatted. Two formats are defined: one that hides what the secret is, and one that is a plain fixed string, recommended to be limited to characters that every implementation can store. The document also says plainly that sharing one secret among a group of peers is a bad idea, because a group member can record traffic and open it later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A critical consideration is how to ensure the randomness of the shared key. Quantum computers are able to perform Grover's algorithm, which effectively halves the size of a symmetric key. In addition, an adversary impersonating the server, even with a conventional computer, can perform a dictionary search over plausible key values. The strongest practice is to ensure that the key contains at least 256 bits of entropy, which provides 128 bits of post-quantum security while also providing security against conventional dictionary attacks. That is the security equivalent of Category 5 in the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Call for Proposals. Deriving the key from a password, a name or another low-entropy source is not secure because of these known attacks.

With this protocol, the computed SK_d is a function of the shared key. Assuming the key has sufficient entropy, for example at least 2^256 possible values, even if an attacker were able to recover the rest of the inputs to the pseudorandom function, it would be infeasible to use Grover's algorithm to recover the SK_d value. All the keys that are a function of SK_d, which include all child security association keys and all keys for subsequent IKE security associations created when the initial one is rekeyed, are therefore quantum secure, assuming the key had enough entropy and the subkeys are sufficiently long.

An attacker with a quantum computer that can decrypt the initial IKE security association has access to everything exchanged over it, such as the identities of the peers, configuration parameters and all negotiated IPsec information including traffic selectors, with the exception of the cryptographic keys used by the IPsec security associations, which are protected by the shared key. Deployments that treat this information as sensitive, or that send other sensitive data such as cryptographic keys over IKE security associations, must rekey the IKE security association before the sensitive information is sent. It is possible to create a childless IKE security association as specified in RFC 6023, which prevents child security association configuration information from being transmitted in the original IKE security association that is not protected by the shared key. Some information, such as peer identities, feature notifications and vendor IDs, cannot be hidden from this attack even with the extra rekey.

The policy should also be set to negotiate only quantum secure symmetric algorithms. The document lists the defined IKEv2 and IPsec algorithms that should not be used, because they are known to provide less than 128 bits of post-quantum security: any IKEv2 encryption algorithm, pseudorandom function or integrity algorithm with a key size less than 256 bits; any ESP transform with a key size less than 256 bits; and the two functions PRF_AES128_XCBC and PRF_AES128_CBC, which, even though they can take an input key of arbitrary size, convert it into a 128-bit key for internal use.

Section 3 requires the initiator to abort the initial exchange if using the keys is mandatory but the responder does not include USE_PPK. In that situation the initiator leaves a half-open IKE security association on the responder, because the IKE_SA_INIT completed successfully from the responder's point of view. It will eventually expire, but if the initiator keeps retrying at a high enough rate the responder may treat it as a denial-of-service attack and take protective measures. It is recommended that the initiator cache the negative result and not try again for some time; waiting at least a few minutes will not cause the responder to treat it as an attack. This situation would most likely be a result of misconfiguration, and some reconfiguration of the peers would probably be needed.

If using the keys is optional for both peers and they authenticate with digital signatures, an attacker in between with a quantum computer able to break public key operations in real time can mount a downgrade attack by removing the USE_PPK notification from the IKE_SA_INIT and forging digital signatures in the subsequent exchange. If using the keys is mandatory for at least one peer, or if a preshared key mode is used for authentication, the attack is detected and the security association is not created.

If using the keys is mandatory for the initiator, an attacker able to eavesdrop and inject packets can prevent the creation of a security association by intercepting the request containing USE_PPK and injecting a forged response without it. If the forged packet arrives before the responder's genuine response, the initiator would abort the exchange. To thwart this, it is recommended that, when using the keys is mandatory for the initiator and the received response does not contain USE_PPK, the initiator does not abort immediately. It waits for more response messages, retransmitting the request as if no responses had been received, until either a received message contains USE_PPK or the exchange times out. If none of the responses contains USE_PPK, the exchange is aborted.

If using a key is optional for both peers, then in case of misconfiguration, such as a mismatched identifier, the security association will be created without protection against quantum computers. It is advised that if a key was configured but not used for a particular security association, implementations should audit this event.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared key has to be genuinely random and long: at least 256 bits of entropy, which a quantum attacker can only halve. The RFC also explains what a quantum attacker still learns, which is the metadata of the first handshake but not the keys protecting the traffic, and how to rekey before sending anything sensitive. It warns that an optional key can be removed by an attacker, and that a mismatched configuration silently produces an unprotected tunnel, so the audit matters.

sections.title: Registry Entries
sections.content:
The document defines three new Notify Message Types in the IKEv2 Notify Message Types, Status Types subregistry: 16435 for USE_PPK, 16436 for PPK_IDENTITY and 16437 for NO_PPK_AUTH.

IANA has also created a new subregistry titled IKEv2 Post-quantum Preshared Key ID Types under the IKEv2 Parameters registry, for the identifier types used in the PPK_IDENTITY notification. The initial contents are PPK_ID_OPAQUE with the value 1 and PPK_ID_FIXED with the value 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new notification numbers are registered for the messages this RFC adds, and a small new registry holds the two identifier formats.
